s03.client_chat.cc_001: Good evening. My name is Bram Merckx. I don't know how to write a message like this so I will just write it.
s03.client_chat.cc_002: My son Sander died on the ninth of November. He was eighteen. They found him in the old lock-house on the Coupure, and the room he was found in was not the room of a boy who wanted to be there.
s03.client_chat.cc_003: They tried to tell me it was suicide. I know my son. It was not suicide.
s03.client_chat.cc_004: There was a man following him. Dieter Vos. For two months, outside the school, outside the bindery. Sander photographed his car. Sander called him at ten past ten that night and twenty-nine minutes later he sent me a message asking for help. I did not hear it come in. I was asleep in the next room.
s03.client_chat.cc_005: They charged Vos and then they let him go again in January because a photograph of a car is not evidence. So now there is nothing. A file with my son's name on it and nothing inside.
s03.client_chat.cc_006: I have his phone. The police took what they wanted from it and gave it back, and I have not been able to open a single thing on it since. I bind books for a living. I am not equipped for this.
s03.client_chat.cc_007: Will you look at it? Properly. I can pay — not much, but properly.
s03.client_chat.cc_007.accept: Give me access to the phone.
s03.client_chat.cc_007.decline: I'm not the right person for this.
s03.client_chat.cc_008: Thank you. The boy at the computer shop on the corner set it up so you can reach it from wherever you are — it's connected now, it's on the desk in front of me. I haven't touched anything on it. I wouldn't know how.
s03.client_chat.cc_009: Start with that night if you can. I keep thinking if I understood those twenty-nine minutes I would understand all of it.
s03.interstitial.is1_001: You're further in one evening than they got in two months.
s03.interstitial.is1_002: I should say something, in case it matters. Sander was not unhappy. Everyone keeps deciding afterwards that he must have been, because it makes the ending tidy. He was quiet. There's a difference and I'm tired of explaining it.
s03.interstitial.is1_003: He read four books a week. He was writing one. Who does that if they've given up?
s03.interstitial.is2_001: Vos's daughter. Yes. I know about Lieve.
s03.interstitial.is2_002: She drowned in March, in the same stretch of water, and the man lost his mind, and he decided a boy from the same school must have had something to do with it. That is what grief does when nobody gives it anywhere to go.
s03.interstitial.is2_003: I felt sorry for him for about a week. Then he started sitting outside my shop.
s03.interstitial.is2_004: Keep going. Whatever he was doing out there, he was doing it to my son as well.
s03.interstitial.is3_002: You were sending me a line every hour and now it's been most of a day, so either you've stopped or you've found something you don't want to type.
s03.interstitial.is3_003: You can tell me. I've already had the worst phone call there is. Nothing you say tonight is going to be worse than a man on my doorstep at six in the morning.
s03.closing_chat.cl_002: I've read it four times. The chapter list, the dates, the two textbooks. I keep looking for the reading of it where I'm wrong.
s03.closing_chat.cl_003: He underlined how a body behaves in cold water eight days before that girl went into the Coupure. He underlined it in February. She died in March. There isn't another way to hold that.
s03.closing_chat.cl_004: Three of them. A boy from the year above. Dieter's daughter. And an old woman on the Sluizeken I used to sell repairs to — she brought me a hymnal with a broken spine and I gave it back to her free because she was ninety percent of my mother.
s03.closing_chat.cl_005: And then Vos got close, and rather than be a boy who got caught, he made himself the last chapter. He wrote the ending where the detective arrives too late and the wrong man is standing over the body. He wrote it on the second of November and he did it on the ninth. On time. He was always on time.
s03.closing_chat.cl_006: I taught him to sew a signature at seven years old. He had the steadiest hands of anyone in that workshop.
s03.closing_chat.cl_007: Dieter Vos is at home tonight believing the police still think he killed a child. His daughter is still in a file marked accidental. Two other families have a word for what happened to them and the word is wrong.
s03.closing_chat.cl_008: It's mine to decide and I can't decide it. So I'm asking you, because you're the one who read it. What do we do?
s03.closing_chat.cl_008.opt1: All of it. Every name, every date.
s03.closing_chat.cl_008.opt2: Clear Vos. Leave the rest buried.
s03.closing_chat.cl_008.opt3: Nothing. Let him stay your son.
s03.closing_chat.cl_010: Yes. I knew you'd say that and I wanted you to say it, because I couldn't.
s03.closing_chat.cl_011: Dieter is going to hear that a boy he was right about killed his daughter, and that everyone told him he was mad for eight months. I don't know if that's mercy. It's the truth and those aren't the same thing, whatever people say.
s03.closing_chat.cl_012: Half of it, then. The half that lets a living man sleep.
s03.closing_chat.cl_013: I can do that. I can hand over the message he faked and the timings and let them work out that nobody was in that room with him. Dieter gets his life back. And Lieve stays an accident, and Margot Peeters stays bad wiring, and Timo Bracke stays a boy who shouldn't have been on a roof. I'll carry that. It's a small enough thing to carry compared to the rest of it.
s03.closing_chat.cl_015: I've thought about it every hour since you sent me the chapter list, and every hour I decide the same thing and then I look at his handwriting and I stop deciding. Maybe that's the answer and I'm not brave enough to hear it from myself. All right. Nothing.
s03.closing_chat.cl_016: I'm going to close the shop for a while. Thank you for reading him properly. Nobody else did — that's what I keep coming back to. He wrote nine chapters and the only person who ever finished them was a stranger I paid.

s03.mail.gm_001.subject: Sander — check-in note
s03.mail.gm_001.body:
Dear Mr Merckx,

I wanted to write rather than call. Sander has now missed three of our scheduled sessions. I want to stress that he is not in any trouble and his marks are, frankly, the best in the year.

My only observation — and I put it carefully — is that he has become quite withdrawn since the spring. He is polite, he is present, he answers. But there is a distance there that I don't think was there in September.

If you have ten minutes before Christmas I would value them.

Kind regards,
Sanne Coppens
Student Welfare
s03.mail.gm_002.subject: Re: Sander — check-in note
s03.mail.gm_002.body:
Dear Mr Merckx,

Thank you for coming in. I don't want to overstate what I said. Withdrawn is the word I keep landing on, and I know how it sounds coming from a school — half the boys in that year are withdrawn and the other half only wish they were.

What I would say is that he seems to have got very interested in something and very uninterested in everything else, and I have seen that go both ways in seventeen years.

We will keep the Monday slot open for him.

Sanne
s03.mail.gm_003.subject: Your submission — NACHTVEER PRIJS 2025
s03.mail.gm_003.body:
Dear Mr Merckx,

Thank you for submitting THE NIGHT REGISTER (chapters 1–7) to this year's Nachtveer Prize for a first novel.

After careful reading the panel has decided not to take your manuscript forward. I want to be straightforward with you about why, because the discussion was unusual.

Two readers thought the prose the strongest in the entire entry. All four thought the book unpublishable. The objection, put plainly, is that the deaths are described with a precision that reads less like invention than like transcription, and that the novel has no interest whatsoever in the people they happen to. One reader used the word clinical. Another used a stronger word and asked me not to repeat it.

You are eighteen and you can clearly write. That is a real thing to have. But you will need to find something in this book to care about before anyone can publish it.

With regards,
T. Lemmens
Chair of the Panel

s03.notes.note_002.title: SOURCE MATERIAL
s03.notes.note_002.block_001: Grey Volvo V40, plate 1-TKR-449. First seen 12 September, Kortrijksepoortstraat, 15:40.
s03.notes.note_002.block_002: Driver: D. Vos, 47. Crane operator, Rigakaai. Lives Muide, ground floor, one light on until three.
s03.notes.note_002.block_003: Pattern: school gate Tue/Thu, bindery Sat afternoon. Never approaches. Never photographs. Sits.
s03.notes.note_002.block_004: He is not building a case. He has no case to build. He is doing the only thing left, which is to look at me until I do something.
s03.notes.note_002.block_005: This is the most useful thing that has happened to the book. A pursuer who is right and who nobody believes. I could not have invented him — I tried, in chapter four, and he was thin.
s03.notes.note_002.block_006: Working assumption: he goes to the police in the new year and they finally listen, because eventually somebody always does.
s03.notes.note_003.block_001: For whoever gets far enough to open this. I have assumed it would be a stranger. That is not modesty, it is arithmetic: the people who love me are not going to look, and the people who look do not love me.
s03.notes.note_003.block_002: There were three. Timo Bracke in October, from the Zuid roof. Lieve Vos in March, in the Coupure. Margot Peeters in June, on the Sluizeken. I have written all three and the writing is accurate, which was the entire point of doing them.
s03.notes.note_003.block_003: People will want it to be hatred. It was not hatred. I did not know any of them, which is why it could be any of them. A book about murder written by somebody who has only imagined it is a book about imagining, and I did not want to write that book.
s03.notes.note_003.block_004: Vos has been outside for two months. He is right about me and nobody has believed him for eight months and they are going to believe him eventually, and on that day the book stops being a book and becomes evidence, and the thing I made becomes the thing they made of me.
s03.notes.note_003.block_005: So chapter nine. The detective arrives too late, the wrong man is standing over the body, and the book ends the way I want it to end rather than the way a courtroom would end it. Vos will be arrested. That is not cruelty either — he is simply the last piece of material and he has been sitting outside offering himself for two months.
s03.notes.note_003.block_006: Dad: you are going to want the reason. The reason is that I finished it. Nine chapters. There is nothing after nine.
s03.notes.note_004.title: Structure — do not lose this
s03.notes.note_004.block_001: I — The Reader. II — The Shop. III — The Fall. IV — The Man Outside (weak, rewrite). V — The Weight. VI — The Interval. VII — The Slow Room. VIII — The Register. IX — The Detective Arrives.
s03.notes.note_004.block_002: Rule for all nine: nothing goes in that I have not verified. The reader always knows. Vance knew and that is why the Long Way Down still works at seventy years old.

(Interior, echo, water moving somewhere below. A boy's voice, unhurried, reading.)

"…and the detective arrives, as the detective always arrives, at the hour when arriving is a formality. (Pause. Paper.)

"Yeah. That's the last line. That's fine."

(Recording ends.)

s03.cloud.cf_003.body:
V — THE WEIGHT

[epigraph]  p. 214 / 0303

Cold water does not drown a person. Cold water empties them, and the water that follows is a formality. The interval between the two is four minutes on a good day and ninety seconds on the third of March, and the girl in this chapter has ninety seconds and does not know that the number exists…

VII — THE SLOW ROOM

A fire in an old house does not roar. It thinks about it. It goes along a skirting board the way a man goes along a corridor he has been told not to hurry down, and by the time the room is bright the woman in the chair has been asleep for some time…

IX — THE DETECTIVE ARRIVES

The man in the doorway is called Vos and he did not do it. He has been outside for two months, which is what makes him useful: a man seen enough times becomes a man who was there. The detective will arrive at six in the morning, and Vos will already have been arrested at four, and the body on the floor will have arranged itself with great care at some point before midnight…

…and between the two of them the room is telling the only lie it was ever asked to tell.

[END]

s03.reader.h_001: "To be a detective is to arrive after the interesting part and to be paid for describing it."
s03.reader.h_001.note: the whole job, in one line
s03.reader.h_002: "He had been careful in the way that only frightened men are careful, and every careful thing he did was a sentence in the confession he was writing without knowing it."
s03.reader.h_002.note: the mistake is always the caution. never the act.
s03.reader.h_003: "Nobody looks twice at an accident. An accident is the one story the world is desperate to accept."
s03.reader.h_004: "To say goodbye is to be honest for once about the fact that you are not coming back."
s03.reader.h_005: "The narrator has been in the room the entire time. He has told you no lie. He has simply declined, on every page, to say the one true thing."
s03.reader.h_005.note: this is the only honest way to do it
s03.reader.h_006: "A confession made to a reader is not a confession. It is a performance with excellent acoustics."
s03.reader.h_007: "They did not catch him. He finished, and finishing looked so much like being caught that nobody could tell the difference."
s03.reader.h_008: "He chose them the way a carpenter chooses wood: for grain, for dryness, for how it would take the work. Not for what it had done to him. It had done nothing to him. That was the requirement."
s03.reader.h_008.note: Ashgrove understood it and then apologised for understanding it, for ninety pages
s03.reader.h_009: "Immersion in water below 10 °C produces an involuntary gasp reflex within the first three seconds. Where the head is submerged at the moment of immersion, aspiration is effectively unavoidable and incapacitation may precede any conscious attempt to swim."
s03.reader.h_009.note: 3 sec. so the entry matters more than the swimmer.
s03.reader.h_010: "Cold shock is at its most severe between 5 °C and 12 °C. Contrary to public belief the danger is greatest in the first minute, not the tenth: most cold-water fatalities are not exhaustion but aspiration in the opening seconds."
s03.reader.h_011: "Post-mortem, cold-water immersion deaths are commonly recorded as accidental where there is no witness and no external injury. The absence of a struggle is not evidence of the absence of a struggle."
s03.reader.h_011.note: no witness = accidental. that's the finding, written in advance.
s03.reader.h_012: "Deteriorated rubber insulation on pre-1960 domestic wiring will crack at the point of flex, most often where a cable passes behind a skirting board. Ignition in such cases is slow, low and rarely detected until the room above is involved."
s03.reader.h_012.note: slow, low. that's the chapter title.
s03.reader.h_013: "Investigators attribute the majority of such fires to the wiring itself, since the failure point is consumed in the event and cannot be distinguished from a deliberate abrasion of the same insulation."
s03.reader.h_014: "Impact from heights above eight metres onto a hard surface produces injuries indistinguishable, in the great majority of cases, from those of an unwitnessed fall."
s03.reader.h_014.note: eleven floors at the Zuid. more than enough.

s03.ending.truth: The chapter list goes to Inspector Waegeman on a Tuesday and takes eleven weeks to become official. Lieve Vos is reclassified in April; Timo Bracke and Margot Peeters follow in the summer. Dieter Vos is cleared, and then has to live with having been right for eight months while a city called him mad. He writes to Bram twice. Bram answers the second one. The bindery reopens in September with the workshop rearranged so that nobody has to sit where Sander sat.
s03.ending.vos_only: The faked message and the timings go in; nothing else does. Vos is cleared in six weeks and never learns why, only that it was quick. Lieve stays an accident, Margot stays bad wiring, Timo stays a boy who shouldn't have been on a roof. Bram keeps the manuscript in the safe under the guillotine and takes it out perhaps twice a year, and every time he decides again, and every time the decision holds until roughly the following morning.
s03.ending.bury: Nothing is filed. The case stays open and inactive, which in practice means closed, and the only name ever attached to it stays Dieter Vos — never charged again, never cleared either, a man everyone in Ghent knows something about and nobody can say what. Bram sells the bindery in the spring. Sander remains, in every record that exists, an eighteen-year-old who was murdered, which is the ending Sander wrote and the one he got.

s03.notes.f_note_301.title: the man on the corner — for chapter 7
s03.notes.f_note_301.body:
He is there at the same hour and he is not doing anything. That is the whole trick of him. A man doing something is a scene; a man doing nothing, twice, is a threat.

Give him a paper he never reads. Give him the same coat. Do not give him a reason until chapter eleven, and when it comes it should be a disappointing one.

(He is not anybody. Femke asked. He is a device.)
s03.notes.f_note_302.title: watching, how it actually feels
s03.notes.f_note_302.body:
Every book gets this wrong. It is not fear. Fear is an event and this is not an event.

It is that you start narrating yourself. You walk differently because you are being walked at. You choose the long way home not because you are afraid but because you have begun to be interested in what the other person will do, and that is the part nobody writes.

s03.notes.f_note_304.title: the problem with chapter eleven
s03.notes.f_note_304.body:
The reveal is that there is nothing to reveal. He was a man walking to work and the boy built the rest.

The problem is that this is only good if the reader also built it. If I have made him sinister on the page then it is a cheat, and if I have not made him sinister at all then there is no book.

So: everything ominous has to come from the boy noticing it, never from the man doing it. Every single time. Go back through and check.

s03.notes.f_note_308.title: what the father knows
s03.notes.f_note_308.body:
He knows the boy has stopped eating properly and he thinks it is about school. He is wrong but he is wrong in a way that is close enough to be useful to him, so he does not look further.

That is not a failure of love. Write it so nobody reads it as one.
s03.notes.f_note_309.title: ending — three ways
s03.notes.f_note_309.body:
One. He tells somebody and is believed. Too easy and not true to any of it.

Two. He tells somebody and is not believed. Honest, and I have read it forty times.

Three. He does not tell anybody, and the book is about the deciding rather than the telling.

Three. It has to be three. It is harder and it is the only one that is actually about him.
